candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'follow the event over time', with the three-month timescale and the physiotherapist viewpoint, led to following one antipsychotic prescription from the first dose to week 12, including the walking and falls checks in the first fortnight.
candidates.working_title: One antipsychotic prescription, followed for 12 weeks
candidates.core_insight: When an antipsychotic is started for severe distress in a person with dementia, the plan should name the target symptom, the checks in the first fortnight (drowsiness, stiffness, slower walking, falls) and a review within six weeks at which stopping is the first question.
candidates.angle: Most teaching on antipsychotics in dementia is about whether to start. This follows what should happen afterwards, week by week, because the harms build up while the review date is forgotten.
candidates.position: Every antipsychotic started for a person with dementia should have a named target symptom, a review date no later than six weeks and a plan to stop, written on the day it is prescribed.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG97 advises offering antipsychotics to people with dementia only when they are at risk of harming themselves or others, or have agitation, hallucinations or delusions causing severe distress (NICE guideline).
NICE NG97 advises the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time, reassessment at least every 6 weeks, and stopping if there is no clear ongoing benefit (NICE guideline).

Risperidone's UK licence in Alzheimer's dementia covers short-term treatment, up to 6 weeks, of persistent aggression unresponsive to non-drug approaches when there is a risk of harm (UK Summary of Product Characteristics).
Antipsychotics in older people with dementia are associated with sedation, parkinsonism, gait disturbance and falls (trial adverse event data or systematic review).
Antipsychotic use in dementia is associated with increased risk of stroke and death in placebo-controlled trials (meta-analysis; regulatory warnings).
Many people on long-term antipsychotics for behavioural symptoms can have them withdrawn without worsening of behaviour (Cochrane review of withdrawal trials).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Write the review date on the same day you write the first dose of an antipsychotic for someone with dementia.
candidates.visual_idea: Timeline diagram across 12 weeks: day 0 (target symptom named, causes looked for, benefits and harms discussed with the person and family), weeks 1 to 2 (check drowsiness, stiffness, walking and falls), week 6 (review: continue only with clear ongoing benefit, otherwise reduce and stop), week 12 (if still prescribed, reason recorded). Labels only, no invented data. Credit NICE NG97.
candidates.pause: Practitioners recognise the prescription started for one bad week that was still there months later.
candidates.gain: A dated review schedule tied to national guidance that can be copied into a drug chart or care home plan.
candidates.follow: The account turns guidelines into specific, usable steps.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E057 (antipsychotic for personal care as a failed pain plan) and E140 (haloperidol cautions in delirium). This post is about the review timeline after an antipsychotic is started for distress in dementia, not about pain or delirium.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'apply it to the poorest or most isolated person' and the home care worker viewpoint led to asking how dementia support and research fit someone who lives alone with no family carer.
candidates.working_title: Dementia care designed around a carer who is not there
candidates.core_insight: Many people with dementia live alone, and some have no family carer at all, yet trials and services often require or assume a carer, so the evidence and the support fit them least well.
candidates.angle: The exclusion is often written into the rules: the GREAT trial of cognitive rehabilitation named the exclusion of people without a carer as a limitation. The evidence on outcomes for people living alone is mixed, so the argument is about fit and access, not a prediction of harm.
candidates.position: Dementia services and trials should plan for people who live alone without a family carer, rather than treating a carer as a condition of entry.
claims_needing_evidence: A substantial proportion of community-dwelling people with dementia live alone; 51% in a German primary care sample (Eichler 2016, cohort baseline data); UK estimate to be found.
Some people with dementia who live alone have no informal carer; about 9% in the German sample (Eichler 2016).

Dementia intervention trials commonly require a family carer or study partner for inclusion; GREAT required a family carer and listed the exclusion of people without one as a limitation (Clare 2019, HTA report).
In the German sample, people living alone used more professional services and did not differ on measured clinical variables (Eichler 2016).
People with dementia living alone had more unmet needs than those living with others in a UK study (Miranda-Castillo 2010, to check).

candidates.opening_line_draft: Many dementia trials only enrol people who have a family member or friend to act as a study partner.
candidates.visual_idea: Comparison card: left, a care pathway drawn with a person and a carer at every step (appointment, medicines, follow-up call); right, the same pathway for a person living alone, with the carer outline empty and a question at each step: who does this? Drawn icons, no data.
candidates.pause: Home care workers and relatives of people who live alone recognise that letters, calls and medicines plans assume someone else is in the house.
candidates.gain: A clear view of where the gap lies and a question to test any plan: who does this step if there is no family carer?
candidates.follow: The account looks for the people standard pathways miss, and uses evidence to show it.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E010 (people living alone are less likely to be diagnosed). This post is about care and research after diagnosis, not diagnosis rates.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'take a common shortcut and qualify it', with the GP viewpoint and the five-year timescale, pointed to the habit of stopping donepezil once dementia is severe or the person moves into a care home.
candidates.working_title: Stopping donepezil because the dementia is now severe
candidates.core_insight: Severity alone is not a reason to stop a cholinesterase inhibitor such as donepezil; in the DOMINO-AD trial, stopping donepezil in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease was followed by more care home moves in the first year, though not over the next three years.
candidates.angle: The shortcut assumes the drug stops doing anything once dementia is advanced. The trial evidence suggests modest continued benefit for some people, so the decision should rest on side effects, benefit, the person's goals and the stage of illness, not on a test score or a change of address.
candidates.position: Stopping donepezil should be decided on side effects, benefit and the person's goals, not on dementia severity alone; near the end of life, stopping is often reasonable.
claims_needing_evidence: NICE NG97 advises not stopping acetylcholinesterase inhibitors in people with Alzheimer's disease because of disease severity alone (NICE guideline).
In DOMINO-AD, continuing donepezil in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease gave small benefits in cognition and daily function over 12 months compared with stopping (Howard 2012, RCT).

In DOMINO-AD, stopping donepezil roughly doubled the risk of nursing home placement in the first 12 months (hazard ratio 2.09), with no difference over the following 3 years (Howard 2015, secondary and post hoc analyses).
Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause nausea, weight loss, slow heart rate and fainting, which can justify stopping (SmPC; Gill 2009 cohort).

candidates.gain: An evidence-based set of reasons to stop or continue, and the trial result that informs it.
candidates.follow: The account treats deprescribing as a decision with evidence on both sides.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'take a common shortcut and qualify it', the speech and language therapist viewpoint and the quality 'order of events' led to breaking a meal into stages to find where eating fails.
candidates.working_title: Eating difficulty in dementia is often not a swallowing problem
candidates.core_insight: When a person with dementia stops eating well, the difficulty may be at any stage of a meal (noticing the food, recognising it, getting it to the mouth, chewing, or swallowing), and each stage needs a different response.
candidates.angle: The shortcut is to refer for a swallow assessment and change the food texture. Watching one meal and naming the stage that fails often points to simpler responses: prompting, help to start, finger food, fewer distractions or more time.
candidates.position: Before food texture is changed for a person with dementia, someone should watch a meal and record which stage of eating is failing.
claims_needing_evidence: Mealtime difficulties in dementia include problems with attention, recognising food, starting to eat and using cutlery, as well as problems with chewing and swallowing (narrative or systematic reviews).
The type of eating difficulty changes with dementia stage, with swallowing problems more common in later stages (cross-sectional or cohort study).
The Edinburgh Feeding Evaluation in Dementia scale is a validated observational measure of feeding difficulty (scale development papers).
Interventions such as carer training, assistance and changes to the dining environment improved intake in some studies (systematic review).

Chang CC, Roberts BL. J Clin Nurs 2008, feeding difficulty in older adults with dementia (unsure of pages)

candidates.opening_line_draft: A person with dementia who leaves a full plate may have no trouble swallowing at all.
candidates.visual_idea: Diagram of a meal in five labelled stages in a row (notices the food; knows it is food; gets it to the mouth; chews and moves it in the mouth; swallows), each with one sign of difficulty and one response, e.g. 'holds food in the mouth: prompt, check the mouth, give time'. Line drawings of a plate, hand and mouth.
candidates.pause: Nurses, speech and language therapists and care home staff recognise the automatic referral and texture change for someone who needed a prompt.
candidates.gain: A way to observe a meal that locates the problem and points to the right help.
candidates.follow: The account gives observational, practical teaching that changes daily care.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'test a familiar slogan against the evidence' was applied to 'living well with dementia'; the spouse viewpoint and the first month after diagnosis shaped it as a post for a couple who have just heard the diagnosis.
candidates.working_title: What 'living well with dementia' is linked with
candidates.core_insight: In a large meta-analysis, better quality of life in dementia was linked with relationships, social engagement and daily function, and poorer quality of life with depression and poorer physical health, with mostly small associations, so a memory score says little about how well someone is living.
candidates.angle: People often hear a dementia diagnosis as a forecast of misery. The evidence shows quality of life varies widely and is linked with things that can be supported, such as mood, relationships, social contact and health.
candidates.position: Care after a dementia diagnosis should give as much attention to mood, relationships, health and daily activity as to monitoring memory.
claims_needing_evidence: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 198 studies covering 37,639 people with dementia found better quality of life associated with relationships, social engagement and functional ability, and poorer quality of life with poorer physical and mental health, including depression, and poorer carer well-being (Martyr 2018).
Most associations were small (0.1 to 0.29) or negligible (Martyr 2018).
Cognition had only a weak association with quality of life (Martyr 2018 full text; must be verified before use).
The findings are observational associations and do not show that changing one factor will change quality of life (Martyr 2018).
evidence_leads: Martyr A et al. Psychol Med 2018;48:2130-9 (PMID 29734962) and corrigendum 2020 (PMID 32476638)
IDEAL programme, Clare L and colleagues, living well with dementia cohort (unsure of specific paper)

candidates.gain: Evidence that life after diagnosis depends partly on things they can work on, and which ones.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome that patients value and the routine measure misses', with the physiotherapist viewpoint (goal-setting) and the map legend (what a measure stands for), led to a trial in which people's own goals improved while standard scores did not move.
candidates.working_title: The trial where people's own goals improved and the standard scores did not
candidates.core_insight: In the GREAT trial, cognitive rehabilitation at home helped people with early dementia make large gains on everyday goals they chose themselves, while quality of life, mood and cognition scores showed no difference.
candidates.angle: Standard dementia outcome measures are general, and the gains people want are often specific. A trial that measured each person's own goals found a large effect that the usual scales did not detect.
candidates.position: Dementia services and trials should measure progress on the goals people with dementia set for themselves, alongside standard scales.
claims_needing_evidence: GREAT randomised 475 people with mild to moderate Alzheimer's, vascular or mixed dementia to cognitive rehabilitation or usual treatment (Clare 2019).
Cognitive rehabilitation was 10 sessions over 3 months and 4 maintenance sessions over 6 months, at home, delivered mostly by occupational therapists (Clare 2019, HTA report).
Participant-rated goal attainment improved with a large effect at 3 months (Cohen's d 0.97) and 9 months (d 0.94), and carer ratings agreed (Clare 2019).
There were no significant differences in quality of life, mood, self-efficacy or cognition (Clare 2019).
Gains related to the goals directly targeted in therapy (Clare 2019, Int J Geriatr Psychiatry).
Examples of the kinds of goals participants chose (full text; to verify before naming any).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'test a familiar slogan against the evidence' and the quality 'averages' led to testing the claim that antipsychotics do not work in dementia against the trial averages for benefit and harm.
candidates.working_title: Antipsychotics in dementia: the numbers both ways
candidates.core_insight: For severe agitation, aggression or psychosis in dementia, antipsychotics help some people a modest amount on average, and in trials about 1 more person in 100 died over 10 to 12 weeks than with placebo, so they are for severe distress or risk of harm, short term, with review.
candidates.angle: Both slogans, 'they never work' and 'they calm people down', mislead. The accurate picture is a small average benefit, real risks of stroke and death, and some people who clearly benefit. Families asked to agree deserve those numbers.
candidates.position: Families should be given absolute benefits and risks before an antipsychotic is started for a person with dementia, and the drug should be reserved for severe distress or risk of harm.
claims_needing_evidence: In a meta-analysis of 15 placebo-controlled trials of atypical antipsychotics in dementia, death occurred in 3.5% on drug and 2.3% on placebo over about 10 to 12 weeks (Schneider 2005).
The benefit of atypical antipsychotics for aggression and psychosis in dementia is modest on average (Cochrane review; meta-analysis).
Atypical antipsychotics in dementia are associated with increased stroke risk (trial data; regulatory review).
NICE advises antipsychotics only for risk of harm or severe distress from agitation, hallucinations or delusions, after discussing benefits and harms with the person and family (NICE NG97).
Some people whose symptoms respond to risperidone relapse when it is stopped (Devanand 2012, RCT).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the scale' and the community pharmacist viewpoint led from a population cohort of about 81,000 people to the one check a pharmacist or family can make: pulse, dizziness and fainting after a dementia medicine starts.
candidates.working_title: Dementia tablets and a slow pulse
candidates.core_insight: Donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine can slow the heart and cause fainting; in a large Ontario study, people with dementia taking them had more hospital visits for fainting, slow heart rate and pacemaker insertion, so new dizziness, faints or falls should prompt a pulse check.
candidates.angle: These medicines are usually described as well tolerated, and nausea and vivid dreams are the side effects people hear about. The heart effects show up as dizziness, faints and falls that are easy to blame on the dementia.
candidates.position: Anyone starting a cholinesterase inhibitor, and their family, should be told to report dizziness, fainting or new falls, and the pulse should be checked at review.
claims_needing_evidence: In an Ontario cohort of 19,803 community-dwelling older adults with dementia prescribed cholinesterase inhibitors and 61,499 controls, hospital visits for syncope were more frequent in users (31.5 vs 18.6 per 1000 person-years), as were visits for bradycardia, pacemaker insertion and hip fracture (Gill 2009).
This is an observational association that does not prove cause (Gill 2009 design).
Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, insomnia and abnormal dreams (SmPC).
Bradycardia and heart block are listed adverse effects, with caution advised in people with heart conduction problems (SmPC; BNF).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'name the trade-off openly' at the timescale 'the moment of discharge' led to the choice between going home and moving to a care home, which is often discussed as safety against risk.
candidates.working_title: Home or a care home: name both sets of risks
candidates.core_insight: When a care home is proposed for a person with dementia in hospital, both options carry risks and benefits, and the person's own wishes and legal rights belong in the discussion alongside falls and safety.
candidates.angle: Discharge discussions often list the risks of going home (falls, getting lost, being alone) and leave out the costs of the alternative: loss of home, routines and neighbours, and a decision made at the person's lowest point after a long stay. Naming both sides makes the decision fairer.
candidates.position: When a care home move is proposed from hospital for a person with dementia, the team should set out the risks and benefits of both options and the person's wishes, and should record how the decision meets the relevant capacity law.
claims_needing_evidence: In a Scottish cohort of 100 people admitted from home and discharged from an acute hospital to a care home, about 95% had a cognitive disorder or evidence of cognitive impairment, 67% had lived alone, and the median hospital stay was 78.5 days (Harrison 2017).
The commonest reasons for the care home decision were family request, dementia, mobility, falls risk and behavioural concerns (Harrison 2017).
The authors reported no established standards for care home decisions made in hospital (Harrison 2017).

Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a person is not treated as lacking capacity merely for making an unwise decision, and best-interests decisions must consider the person's wishes and the less restrictive option; the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 has similar principles (legislation and codes of practice).
UK discharge guidance advises that long-term care decisions should usually not be made in an acute hospital bed (NHS England or Scottish Government guidance; to check).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'count something nobody counts', the shopping list (a simple tally) and the one-year timescale led to counting how many different GPs a person with dementia sees in a year.
candidates.working_title: Count the doctors: continuity of GP care in dementia
candidates.core_insight: In an English study of 9,324 people with dementia, those who saw the same GP most consistently had fewer medicines, fewer potentially inappropriate prescriptions, less incontinence and fewer emergency admissions over a year; the study shows a link, not proof of cause.
candidates.angle: Continuity is simple to count (how many different GPs saw this person in the past year?) and is associated with safer prescribing in dementia, yet it is rarely part of how practices review their care.
candidates.position: General practices should count and protect continuity for people with dementia, and families can ask for a named usual GP.
claims_needing_evidence: A retrospective cohort of 9,324 people with dementia aged 65 or over in England (2016) found that the highest continuity quartile had fewer prescribed medicines (mean 8.5 vs 9.7) and fewer potentially inappropriate prescriptions (2.1 vs 2.5) than the lowest (Delgado 2022).

By week 16 there were 7 deaths with mirtazapine and 1 with placebo; a post hoc analysis gave p = 0.065 (Banerjee 2021).
The authors concluded the data do not support mirtazapine for agitation in dementia (Banerjee 2021).
Mirtazapine is prescribed for agitation in dementia in practice (Banerjee 2021 introduction; background only).

candidates.working_title: Driving after a dementia diagnosis: the law and the plan

candidates.working_title: If someone with dementia goes missing, report it at once
candidates.core_insight: There is no rule that a person must be missing for 24 hours before police will take a report, and for people with dementia longer time missing is linked with harm, so report quickly and keep a prepared form with a recent photo and places they may head for.

Getting lost was a low-frequency event, estimated at 0.5% of the regional dementia population (same study).
The Herbert Protocol is a scheme used by UK police forces in which families record information about a person with dementia to share if they go missing (police force guidance).

candidates.working_title: What families should be told to expect in advanced dementia
candidates.core_insight: In a US study of 323 care home residents with advanced dementia, most developed eating problems and many had fevers or pneumonia over 18 months, and residents whose families understood this expected course were much less likely to have burdensome treatments near the end of life.
candidates.angle: Advanced dementia is a terminal illness, but its usual course is often not explained, so each complication arrives as a surprise and leads to hospital transfers. Knowing what to expect changed the care people received.
candidates.position: Families of people with advanced dementia should be told clearly which complications to expect and what care will be offered when they happen.
claims_needing_evidence: Over 18 months, 54.8% of 323 residents with advanced dementia died; the probability of an eating problem was 85.8%, a febrile episode 52.6% and pneumonia 41.1% (Mitchell 2009).

40.7% had at least one burdensome intervention (hospital admission, emergency department visit, parenteral therapy or tube feeding) in the last 3 months of life (Mitchell 2009).
Residents whose proxies understood the prognosis and expected complications were much less likely to have burdensome interventions (adjusted OR 0.12) (Mitchell 2009).
Few proxies reported that a physician had explained the expected complications (Mitchell 2009 full text; to verify).
The cohort was in US nursing homes; applicability to UK care homes to be stated (UK cohort to compare).

candidates.core_insight: For people with advanced dementia who are eating less, tube feeding has not been shown to prolong life, prevent aspiration pneumonia or heal pressure sores, and careful help to eat by hand for comfort is the recommended approach.
candidates.angle: Tube feeding is often presented as the alternative to letting someone starve. The evidence describes a different choice: continued careful hand feeding for comfort, taste and company, or a tube with burdens and no shown benefit.
candidates.position: Tube feeding should not be offered routinely to people with advanced dementia; careful hand feeding for comfort should be offered and continued.
claims_needing_evidence: Studies of tube feeding in advanced dementia have not shown longer survival, prevention of aspiration pneumonia, better nutrition or healing of pressure ulcers (Finucane 1999 review; Cochrane reviews).
The American Geriatrics Society does not recommend feeding tubes for older adults with advanced dementia and advises careful hand feeding (AGS 2014 position statement).
UK guidance addresses oral feeding difficulties and decisions near the end of life (Royal College of Physicians 2010).
Tube feeding can involve burdens such as tube displacement, discomfort, use of restraint and hospital visits (AGS 2014; observational studies).

candidates.working_title: Exercise in dementia: fitter, but not a treatment for memory
candidates.core_insight: In the UK DAPA trial of 494 people with mild to moderate dementia, four months of moderate to high intensity exercise improved fitness but did not slow cognitive decline; cognitive scores in the exercise group were slightly worse at 12 months, by an amount too small to notice.
candidates.angle: Exercise is widely promoted as protecting the brain. For people who already have dementia, the largest trial found it helped fitness, not memory. That is a reason to offer exercise for strength, mobility and enjoyment, and to be accurate about what it will do.
candidates.position: Offer exercise to people with dementia for fitness, strength and enjoyment, without promising that it will slow memory loss.
claims_needing_evidence: DAPA randomised 494 people with mild to moderate dementia to a 4-month moderate to high intensity aerobic and strength programme with support, or usual care (Lamb 2018).
At 12 months, ADAS-cog scores were slightly worse in the exercise group (difference about 1.4 points), judged not clinically important (Lamb 2018).
Physical fitness improved in the short term with exercise (Lamb 2018).
There were no clear differences in secondary outcomes such as activities of daily living and quality of life (Lamb 2018; to verify).
Exercise reduces falls in older people living in the community (Sherrington 2019 Cochrane); evidence specific to people with dementia is less certain (to check).

Forbes D et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015, exercise programmes for people with dementia

candidates.working_title: Music and dementia: what it helps and what it does not
candidates.core_insight: A 2025 Cochrane review of 30 trials found that music-based therapy probably improves depressive symptoms slightly and may reduce overall behavioural problems at the end of treatment, but probably does not reduce agitation or aggression, and no lasting effect was shown after sessions ended.
candidates.angle: Music is often promoted as calming for people with dementia. The trials support a narrower claim: a small lift in mood while sessions continue. That points to music as a regular part of daily life for enjoyment and mood, and away from music as the answer to agitation.
candidates.position: Offer music regularly for mood and enjoyment; do not rely on it as the treatment for agitation.
claims_needing_evidence: The 2025 Cochrane review included 30 studies with 1,720 participants (van der Steen 2025).
Compared with usual care, music-based interventions probably improve depressive symptoms slightly at the end of treatment (moderate-certainty evidence) (van der Steen 2025).
They may improve overall behavioural problems (low-certainty evidence) (van der Steen 2025).
They likely do not improve agitation or aggression (moderate-certainty evidence) (van der Steen 2025).
There was no evidence of effects four or more weeks after treatment ended (van der Steen 2025).
Included interventions had at least five sessions and most studies were in care homes or other institutions (van der Steen 2025).

candidates.working_title: What worked in 69 care homes: training, activity and a medicines review
candidates.core_insight: In the WHELD trial in 69 UK nursing homes, training staff in person-centred care and social interaction, with an antipsychotic review, improved residents' quality of life, agitation and other symptoms by small amounts and cost less than usual care.
candidates.angle: The intervention was ordinary care done systematically: staff trained in person-centred care, more social contact and activity, and a champion in each home to keep it going. The result that went the other way: antipsychotic use was already low and did not fall.
candidates.position: Care homes can improve residents' quality of life and reduce agitation with structured person-centred training and activity programmes, and should expect small but real gains.
claims_needing_evidence: WHELD was a cluster RCT in 69 UK nursing homes; 847 people were randomised and 553 completed 9 months (Ballard 2018).

The intervention improved quality of life (DEMQOL-Proxy, effect size 0.24), agitation (CMAI, 0.23) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH, 0.30), with the largest benefits in moderately severe dementia (Ballard 2018).
Positive care interactions increased (Ballard 2018).
Antipsychotic use was low and stable in both groups and was not reduced (Ballard 2018).
The intervention reduced costs compared with usual care (Ballard 2018).

candidates.working_title: When a person with dementia asks for someone who has died
candidates.core_insight: When a person with dementia asks for a parent or partner who died long ago, repeating the news can bring fresh grief each time; a UK inquiry set out a range of responses, from gentle truth to responding to the feeling behind the question, and asked that any choice serve the person.
candidates.angle: Families feel torn between honesty and kindness. The inquiry did not give a single rule; it described a range and a test: what helps this person now?
candidates.position: Carers should respond first to the feeling or need behind the question; any departure from the literal truth should be for the person's benefit, not the carer's convenience.
claims_needing_evidence: The Mental Health Foundation's 2016 inquiry on truth and lying in dementia care gathered views from people with dementia, carers and professionals (MHF 2016 report).
The inquiry described a range of responses, from truth-telling and looking for the meaning of the question to going along with the person and, as a last resort, lying (MHF 2016; to verify wording).
The inquiry recommended person-centred responses in the person's interests (MHF 2016; to verify).
Repeating news of a death to a person with dementia can cause renewed distress (MHF 2016 or qualitative studies; to verify).

candidates.working_title: Behind distressed behaviour: boredom and loneliness
candidates.core_insight: In a study of care home residents with dementia and behaviour problems, the most common unmet needs were boredom or lack of stimulation, loneliness and need for company, and lack of meaningful activity, so a plan for distress should include company and occupation.
candidates.angle: Pain and physical causes rightly come first when assessing distress, and the earlier collection covered them. This finding adds the next question: what is this person doing all day, and with whom?
candidates.position: Every assessment of distressed behaviour in dementia should ask about boredom, loneliness and activity, and the plan should address them.
claims_needing_evidence: In 89 residents with dementia and behaviour problems in six Maryland nursing homes, an average of three unmet needs per resident was identified, with boredom or sensory deprivation, loneliness or need for social interaction, and need for meaningful activity the most prevalent (Cohen-Mansfield 2015).
The Unmet Needs Model proposes that behaviour problems in dementia arise from needs the person can no longer communicate or meet (Cohen-Mansfield 2015).
Care home residents with dementia spend much of the day without activity (observational study; to verify).

candidates.working_title: Who the new Alzheimer's antibody drugs were tested on
candidates.core_insight: When the lecanemab trial's rules were applied to older people with early Alzheimer's disease in a US population study, only 19 of 237 (about 8 in 100) would have been eligible, mainly because of other health conditions and brain scan findings.
candidates.angle: Coverage of the new drugs often speaks as if they apply to most people with Alzheimer's disease. The trial population was selected, and typical older people with memory problems and other conditions mostly fall outside it, which limits what the results can tell them.
candidates.position: Trial results for anti-amyloid drugs apply to a narrow group, and conversations with older people should start from whether they resemble that group.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 237 Mayo Clinic Study of Aging participants (mean age 80.9) with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia and raised brain amyloid, 112 (47.3%) met the lecanemab trial's inclusion criteria and 19 (8%) remained after exclusion criteria (Pittock 2023).
Common exclusions related to other chronic conditions and neuroimaging findings (Pittock 2023).
97.5% of the sample were White, which limits generalisability (Pittock 2023).
In Clarity AD, lecanemab slowed decline on the 18-point CDR-SB by 0.45 points at 18 months, and ARIA with swelling occurred in 12.6% vs 1.7% (van Dyck 2023).
MHRA licensing and NICE decisions on lecanemab and donanemab (state only as dated fact if used, without inferring a position).

candidates.working_title: Activities matched to what a person can still do
candidates.core_insight: Activities matched to a person's past interests and current abilities, and set up so they can succeed, can reduce distress and ease carers' days; a pilot trial of an occupational therapy approach, the Tailored Activity Program, found fewer behavioural symptoms at home.
candidates.angle: Advice to 'keep them busy' fails when the task is too hard, too childish or chosen by someone else. The tested approach starts with an occupational therapist working out what the person can still do and used to enjoy, then breaks an activity into steps a carer can set up.
candidates.position: People with dementia living at home should have access to occupational therapy that tailors activities to their abilities and interests, and carers should be shown how to set them up.
claims_needing_evidence: A randomised pilot trial of the Tailored Activity Program in 60 families found fewer behavioural symptoms and benefits for carers compared with a wait-list control (Gitlin 2008; verify outcomes).
The programme involves occupational therapists assessing abilities and interests and prescribing activities with instructions for carers (Gitlin 2008).
NICE NG97 recommends offering activities tailored to the person's preferences to promote wellbeing (NICE guideline).
Later, larger trials of the programme had mixed results (to check before any claim of effect is made).

candidates.working_title: When the person insists nothing is wrong
candidates.core_insight: Reduced awareness of one's own difficulties is a common feature of Alzheimer's disease and comes from the illness itself, so arguing about the diagnosis rarely helps, and support can be arranged around the task rather than the label.
candidates.angle: Families often spend energy trying to get the person to accept the diagnosis. Knowing that awareness itself can be affected by the illness allows a different approach: agree on the practical task, such as a check-up or help with bills.
candidates.position: Families and clinicians should treat reduced awareness as a symptom and plan support around it, rather than making acceptance of the diagnosis a condition of help.
claims_needing_evidence: Impaired awareness (anosognosia) is common in Alzheimer's disease, with prevalence estimates varying widely by method (review).
Awareness can differ across areas, for example memory compared with daily activities (review).
Reduced awareness is associated with the brain changes of the disease (neuroimaging review).
Reduced awareness is associated with higher carer strain (observational study; to check).
Practical communication advice (focus on the task, avoid arguing) comes from carer guidance and is weaker evidence; label it as practical advice.

candidates.working_title: Coloured plates and a small study
candidates.core_insight: In a small study of nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease, changing from white to high-contrast red plates and cups was followed by more eating and much more drinking, a follow-up found high-contrast blue worked too, and low-contrast colours did not.
candidates.angle: Contrast, not the colour red, seemed to make the difference. The evidence is small, but the change is cheap and harmless, so it is reasonable to try while watching whether intake changes.
candidates.position: For a person with advanced dementia who eats and drinks poorly, high-contrast plates and cups are a low-cost change to try, with intake noted before and after.
claims_needing_evidence: The study included nine men with advanced Alzheimer's disease in long-term care, over 30 days with white tableware at baseline and afterwards and high-contrast red tableware in between (Dunne 2004).
Mean increases were 25% for food and 84% for liquid with red compared with white tableware, and 8 of 9 participants ate or drank more (Dunne 2004).
In a follow-up, high-contrast blue increased intake, while low-contrast red and low-contrast blue did not (Dunne 2004).
People with severe Alzheimer's disease have reduced contrast sensitivity (Dunne 2004 background; source study to cite).
Whether larger studies have replicated the finding (to search before use).

candidates.working_title: A year of support after diagnosis: Scotland's standard and its reach
candidates.core_insight: Scotland's standard says people newly diagnosed with dementia should receive at least a year of post-diagnostic support from a named link worker, and the published measure counts how many of the estimated new diagnoses were referred, which shows how far the support reaches.
candidates.angle: The standard is one of the clearest post-diagnostic commitments in the UK, built on a five-part model (understanding the illness, peer support, community connections, planning for future decisions, planning for future care). Its measure uses estimated new cases as the denominator, so people never diagnosed, or never referred, show up as a gap.
candidates.position: Post-diagnostic support should be judged by how many people with dementia receive it, and the Scottish measure should be read as a measure of reach.
claims_needing_evidence: Since 2013, a Scottish standard has stated that people newly diagnosed with dementia will receive a minimum of one year of post-diagnostic support coordinated by a named link worker (Scottish Government; Public Health Scotland).
The support is based on Alzheimer Scotland's 5 Pillars model (Alzheimer Scotland 2011).

Public Health Scotland reports the percentage of the estimated number of people newly diagnosed who were referred for post-diagnostic support [N to verify], and the percentage of those who received at least a year [N to verify] (PHS annual publication).
The denominator is an estimate of new cases, not a count of recorded diagnoses (PHS methodology).
